entry.title: Show HN: Local Graph for Your Agents (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: We all use different agentic systems, bots, chats, and so on. One day I realized that I need to copy context between the apps. It is annoying. So I created a trivial local MCP which sits on top of SQLite and exposes Cypher so LLM can query anything. Also LLM can define a schema if it understands it needs new nodes or edges. How do I use it: 1. I've scanned all my documents and stored passports, driver licences and all kind of contracts for my apartment, insurance and so on. And not only mine - the entire family. 2. I've extracted all the key date and values. Also gemini extracted all the personal relations. Like "Alex is-a-child-of Bob". "Bob is-married-to Anna". So i can ask "give me a passport number of my son" and it gives it back instantly. It might not be a big deal, but it is very convenient. 3. It stores all the projects I'm working on, key steps and decisions. 4. And the most important thing - it works from anywhere. I can ask Hermes i telegram to remind me when my insurance ends or I can reference my project in ClaudeCode just by name and it will get the entire history from Antigravity. I would be happy if you guys find it useful. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50562818 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

entry.title: Show HN: An open-source harness for Android devs in the terminal (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: This open-source TUI and CLI allows running the workflows that android devs run every day without leaving the terminal and each one in their own worktree. You can see the agents working in a control pane with different status. The TUI will inform you when it needs your help. You can: 1. Create a Pull Request from a ticket, the harness does a plan -> code -> review workflow. You can decide the model per state. 2. Auto fix the ticket comments, the harness fetches the PR comments and show it in the dashboard. You can previsualize and approve or request a new fix. 3. Review the diff, the TUI has a beauty diff viewer so you can review the code without leaving the terminal. 4. Open the worktree in Android Studio or claude code directly from the TUI. 5. Permission and budget management: you can auto approve comments or approve once. You can also set a spend limit per stage. It is optimized for android: 1. Only one agent at a time can take control of the emulator. 2. The worktree creation, all git operations and PR information is deterministic and handled by the harness taking into consideration how Android projects are built. 3. Open the worktree in Android Studio. 4. Open the emulator from the TUI. Caveats: For now it only works for Claude Code. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50562696 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

entry.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) - An open-source developer tool for designers (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here's a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren't mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That's why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you've built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works... Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is. This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection - which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt. We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They're almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I've made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that's already been built. The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams. We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We're so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code! The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day! Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50562320 Points: 12 # Comments: 2

entry.title: Show HN: Watch weight-space programming in action with WebGPU (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
